images.title: Test each bag weight
images.purpose: Recap that a bag weight works only if it divides both quantities, using a small test table for 18 kg and 30 kg.
images.composition: One small table with 3 data rows in the centre of the frame, framed by white space, with one caption beneath.
exact_structure: A table with 3 columns headed bag weight, 18 kg, 30 kg; the 18 kg header is teal (#0072B2), the 30 kg header is amber (#E69F00).
Row 1: 5 kg; under 18 kg a vermilion (#D55E00) cross; under 30 kg a green (#009E73) tick.
Row 2: 6 kg; under 18 kg a green (#009E73) tick; under 30 kg a green (#009E73) tick. This whole row is shaded light reddish purple (#CC79A7).
Row 3: 9 kg; under 18 kg a green (#009E73) tick; under 30 kg a vermilion (#D55E00) cross.
Exactly 4 ticks and 2 crosses in total.
Below the table, one caption: 6 kg divides both.
rejection: any tick or cross in the wrong cell (5 divides 30 but not 18, 9 divides 18 but not 30, 6 divides both)
any row other than the 6 kg row highlighted
more or fewer than 3 data rows
images.takeaway: A bag weight must divide both quantities, and the greatest weight that passes both tests is the HCF.
images.description: A test table for bag weights 5, 6 and 9 kg against 18 kg and 30 kg, where only 6 kg gets two ticks.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video for this concept.
images.teaching_notes: Read each row as a test against both farms; a single cross rules the weight out.

image_decisions.why: A compact test table recaps the check every trial weight must pass in the practice.
